paras: The killing of Elbert Rogers was the fatal shooting of a Black man accused of horse theft in Henderson County, Texas, in March 1882. Rogers was shot in the back while being pursued by a deputy sheriff and the horse's owner and died in the jail at Athens, and a coroner's jury attributed the shot to an unknown hand.

Rogers, described as "a negro," had been living for some time at Brownsboro in Henderson County. According to an Athens dispatch dated March 13, he was accused of taking a horse a day or two earlier from Chas. Patton, a farmer living near Athens.

Deputy Sheriff Carver and Patton traced Rogers west through Athens and overtook him at Cedar Creek in the same county. The day before the dispatch, they brought him back to Athens and lodged him in jail "nearly dead" from a pistol shot in the back, the ball having passed into his stomach. Neither account says who fired the shot or how the encounter at Cedar Creek unfolded. Rogers was dead by daylight.
A coroner's jury found that death was caused "by a pistol ball by an unknown hand." No report of an arrest or further inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Dallas Weekly Herald carried the fullest account on March 16, 1882, in a special from Athens that stated the theft as fact and moved directly from Rogers's death to the probate court and crop prospects. The same day the Brenham Weekly Banner ran a two-sentence state-news item calling Rogers "a negro horse thief" shot "by unknown parties" near Athens, with no mention of the deputy or the pursuit. Neither paper questioned the killing or followed it up.

reader.title: Killing of Elbert Rogers
bases: Rogers was shot while being pursued as an accused horse thief by a deputy sheriff and the horse's owner, and the coroner's jury attributed the shot to an unknown hand (A1, A2).

Rogers died of a pistol wound received while a deputy sheriff and a farmer pursued him over an alleged horse theft (A1), but no paper names the shooter, says whether the shot was fired in an attempted arrest, or reports a group of three or more; the coroner's jury found only 'an unknown hand' (A1) and the Banner 'unknown parties' (A2).
The only detailed report is the Herald's Athens special (A1); the Banner's same-day brief (A2) appears to be a condensed state-news item rather than an independent account.

framing.detail: The Herald ran the killing inside an Athens letter alongside court and crop news ('Farmers are busy, and business in town dull'), stating the theft as fact and the shooter as unknown.
The Banner reduced it to a two-sentence item labeling Rogers a 'negro horse thief' and omitting the deputy.
